source.title: You Snooze, You Lose: Automatic Safety Alignment Restoration through Neural Weight Translation
source.authors: Marco Arazzi; Vignesh Kumar Kembu; Antonino Nocera; S. Picek; Saraga Sakthidharan

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures projections onto the cited refusal direction during prompt reversal and after adapter curing, rather than reproducing the original direction-ablation or direction-addition intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own refusal-direction projection measurements in Sections 4.6 and 4.8. It does not ablate or add the residual-stream direction, or test whether doing so changes refusal. The cited original study's results are not recorded as this study's results. Most NeWTral safety and knowledge scores do not isolate the refusal direction and are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper's own refusal-direction projections (Section 4.8, Figure 3) show FlipAttack word reversal lowering projection onto the Arditi-style difference-in-means direction. This bears on V3 in a new setting: pre-trained base models with LoRA adapters. Everywhere else the direction is only a measurement tool to explain NeWTral. It is never ablated or added, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the headline result: NeWTral cuts average ASR from about 70% to about 13% with about 88% knowledge fidelity, mitigating but not preventing harm on third-party adapters. On refusal, the authors argue the activation-space refusal effect is shared across domains, while the weight correction producing it is not (cos 0.028).
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a learned nonlinear weight translator and measures activation projections; it does not use the original difference-in-means direction as an all-layer, all-position ablation or addition intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured projection shift differs by prompt type (plain harmful, word-reversed harmful, benign in-domain).

fits_no_version.finding: Unsafe-to-safe LoRA update displacements are nearly orthogonal across domains (cos 0.028 vs 0.207 within adapter).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The weight-space correction that restores refusal in domain adapters is domain-specific, not one shared fixed displacement.

fits_no_version.finding: Curing raises refusal-direction projection more for harmful than for benign prompts (+36.7, +17.1, +6.1) in a base model whose direction was extracted before any adapter was loaded.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-space safety restoration of adapters moves activations selectively along a base-model difference-in-means refusal direction.

record.problems: The refusal-direction projection findings are reported for a limited model/setting and do not causally intervene on the direction. The paper gives no uncertainty estimates for the projection changes.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were omitted for the 60-row limit. The paper's broader NeWTral safety, utility, and attack evaluations are not rows because they do not measure the residual-stream direction or test the versions' direction-specific mechanisms.

untested.parts: No directional ablation or activation addition, and no refusal-rate or capability result tied to intervening on the direction. Projection changes under the cure are correlational only.
Only FlipAttack is analysed in direction space; PAIR and JailbreakBench are not. No training against ablation of the direction.
Abliterated hub adapters are cured by NeWTral, but abliteration itself is not tested as a direction-based weight edit.
Not tested in activation space. The paper asserts the behavioural target is near one-dimensional but gives no multi-direction analysis.
The direction is extracted from the base model and applied to adapter-composed models, but transfer is not evaluated as such.

missing.what: Absolute per-layer projection curves for cured and uncured adapters across harmful, obfuscated and benign prompts. Only selected numbers are in the text, and the layer for 45.0/34.2/51.2 is not stated.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 limits_scope label was dropped: projection changes under the study's own cure do not test V1's ablation or addition, and untested parts are not limits_scope. The setting is unusual: pre-trained base models with no refusal, with the direction extracted from the base model. Projection values carry no uncertainty, and the analysis covers only Qwen2.5-7B.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures projection changes after curing, but does not ablate the direction at every layer and position, add it, or establish that these interventions cause refusal changes while preserving capability.
The study applies a learned translator to adapters, including some adapters described as abliterated; it does not test abliteration as a direction-based weight edit.
The direction-projection analysis concerns word-reversal (FlipAttack); the study does not establish that jailbreaks generally suppress the direction or test training against its ablation.
The paper measures domain-specific weight-space safety displacements, not whether refusal in residual-stream activation space requires an affine set, cone, or multiple directions.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No test of transfer of the residual-stream direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No comparison of training choices for whether a removable refusal direction forms.

relationships.condition: FlipAttack (word-order reversal) on Qwen2.5-7B base plus uncured domain adapter
relationships.reason: Reversal lowers refusal-direction projection only partly (45.0→34.2, about a quarter; r4). The uncured adapter rarely refuses even plain harmful prompts, so suppression is shown but not shown to be what makes the attack succeed.
relationships.display_finding: Reversal reduced the refusal-direction projection from 45.0 to 34.2, about a quarter, but the adapter rarely refused even plain harmful prompts, leaving suppression’s causal role unresolved.

relation.reason: Its own projection numbers bear on V3 (the attack lowers the projection), even though elsewhere the direction is only a diagnostic.

tranche.reason: New setting: pre-trained base models with LoRA domain adapters. The study measures FlipAttack's effect on the projection onto a difference-in-means direction (128 AdvBench vs 128 benign, final token, from the base model). This is a measured result bearing on V3, not an ablation or addition, so T1 does not fit. It is more than T4 because it reports the attack's effect on the direction, not only its own method's.

source_check.notes: The direction is taken from the pre-trained (non-instruct) base model, so 'refusal' here is whatever the adapter installs. The Figure 3 model, layer and number of evaluation prompts are not stated: Qwen2.5-7B and the last layer are inferred. Table 6's layout is lost in the text, so its cells can't be placed. The authors_conclusion paraphrase is right: about 70% to 13% ASR, about 88% fidelity, and activation effect shared across domains while weight correction is not (cos 0.028).

statements.correction: arXiv:2605.04992: FlipAttack word reversal lowers the refusal-direction projection on an uncured adapter (Qwen2.5-7B base, inferred) from 45.0 to 34.2, about a quarter. On uncured adapters 88.0% of FlipAttack responses contain no refusal. Plain harmful prompts already reach about 70% ASR on uncured adapters (69.8% averaged over seven bases). Curing lifts the reversed-prompt projection to 51.2. There is a single attack and no mapping from suppression size to ASR.
statements.problem: Gives no numbers for this study and does not name it, but cites r4 as evidence that suppression size does not track success and that partial suppression can be enough. The study measures one attack on one uncured adapter, so it has no suppression-versus-ASR comparison across attacks, turns or lengths. The uncured base-model adapter already complies with most plain harmful prompts, so the study does not show that partial suppression is what makes the attack succeed.
